news.title: SkillOpt: Agent skills as trainable parameters
news.summary_raw:
AI agents often fail because their instructions, or skills, are manually modified with no guarantee of improvement. Learn how SkillOpt turns skill editing into a training process, making agent behavior more reliable without changing model weights.
The post SkillOpt: Agent skills as trainable parameters appeared first on Microsoft Research.
news.summary: Microsoft Research has developed SkillOpt, a method that trains agent skills as parameters, improving reliability without altering model weights. This enables more effective agent behavior through a trainable editing process.

news.title: 57% of enterprises have watched AI agents be confidently wrong. The fix is an agentic context layer, but who has one?
news.summary_raw: An enterprise AI agent answers with total confidence, but the number is wrong. Nobody catches it until someone traces it back to a stale metric definition or a document the retrieval system never pulled. The model did not fail. The context it was given did.In the past six months, 57% of enterprises traced a confident but wrong AI agent answer to missing or inconsistent business context, and 31% said it happened more than once, according to a VB Pulse June 2026 survey of 101 qualified enterprises
news.summary: 57% of enterprises experienced confident yet wrong AI agent answers, highlighting the need for context layers to improve accuracy. Many cases are linked to missing or inconsistent business context in model definitions or training data.
news.enterprise_use: Review your AI model's context requirements and consider implementing or refining your agentic context layer to ensure accurate and confident responses.

news.summary_raw: Chris Gash/theispot.com The Research The authors synthesized findings from four studies spanning short-story writing, circular-economy solutions, humor caption contests, and collaborative storytelling. AI had the greatest positive effect on individuals with lower […]
news.summary: Research from MIT Sloan found that AI-assisted creativity can lead to more similar ideas at the expense of collective diversity. Four studies showed AI assistance improves individual output quality but homogenizes group ideas.
